Single-Photon Detectors
Fırat Bulduk
16 July 2026

Based on: Eisaman, Fan, Migdall, and Polyakov,
Invited Review Article: Single-photon sources and detectors,
Rev. Sci. Instrum. 82, 071101 (2011)

Why single-photon detectors?

A single photon carries the energy E = hν. At a wavelength of 500 nm this is 4 × 10−19 joule. In a conventional photodiode one photon frees at most one electron-hole pair, and a signal of one electron does not rise above the noise of the readout electronics.

Three fields that measure single photons
Quantum communication
Quantum key distribution encodes each bit of the key in a single photon. Receiving the key means detecting single photons.
Quantum optics
Photonic quantum computing and the characterization of single-photon sources measure light photon by photon.
Faint-light sensing
Fluorescence microscopy, astronomy, and laser ranging receive so little light that the signal arrives as individual photons.
1.Detection Efficiency
η

The detection efficiency is the probability that a photon incident on the detector produces a measurable output signal. It is defined as the ratio of the number of registered counts to the number of incident photons.

Ideal value: 1 (100%).

The three factors
Coupling efficiency
The fraction of the incident photons that reach the active region. Surface reflection, or a dead layer in front, stops the rest before they arrive.
Absorption efficiency
The fraction of those photons that the active region absorbs. Each absorbed photon frees one primary excitation, an electron-hole pair.
Registration efficiency
The fraction of those excitations that grow into an output pulse above the detection threshold. The rest stay below it and never register.
2.Dark-Count Rate
Rdc

The dark-count rate is the number of counts per second that the detector produces in the absence of any photon.

Ideal value: 0.

Sources of dark-count rate
Thermal excitations
Tunnelling
Blackbody radiation
3.Dead Time
τ

The dead time is the interval following a detection event during which the detector is unable to register a subsequent photon. Any photon arriving within this recovery interval is not counted.

Ideal value: 0.

4.Timing Jitter
Δt

The timing jitter is the event-to-event variation in the delay between the arrival of a photon and the generation of the output pulse. It is quoted as the full width at half maximum of the delay distribution.

Ideal value: 0.

5.Photon-Number Resolution
n

Photon-number resolution is the ability of the detector to determine how many photons arrived together in a single incident pulse, distinguishing one photon from two, three, and so on.

Ideal detector: reports the exact photon number.

Image source: photonics.com, By the Numbers: Photon Counting and Number Resolution (a68893)

Three photons arrive in the same pulse, simultaneously (n = 3). What does the electrical output tell us about this photon number?
The review (Eisaman et al., 2011) divides all detectors into two lists:
1 · Non-photon-number-resolving the output does not reveal the number of photons
1Photomultiplier tube (PMT)
2Single-photon avalanche photodiode (SPAD)
3Quantum-dot field-effect transistor detector (QDOGFET)
4Superconducting nanowire detector (SNSPD)
5Up-conversion detector (IR → visible, then SPAD/PMT)
2 · Photon-number-resolving the output reveals the number of photons
1Superconducting tunnel junction (STJ)
2Quantum-dot field-effect transistor detector (QDOGFET)
3Superconducting nanowire, parallel (parallel-SNSPD)
4Transition-edge sensor (TES)
5Visible-light photon counter (VLPC)
6Other PNR detectors (SPAD array, time-multiplexed SPAD, single-SPAD)
Three photons arrive in the same pulse, simultaneously (n = 3). What does the electrical output tell us about this photon number?
Class 1 · Click group (a): no number resolution
One standard pulse, identical for 1, 3, or 10 photons. Reports only that at least one photon arrived.
•PMT photomultiplier tube
•SPAD single-photon avalanche diode
•SNSPD superconducting nanowire
•Up-conversion IR → visible, then SPAD/PMT
Class 2 · Multiplexed group (b): some number resolution
Light split over many independent click elements. Count the ones that fire: three photons give three pulses.
•SPAD array spatial multiplexing
•Time-multiplexed SPAD temporal multiplexing
•Parallel-SNSPD separate wires, digital readout
Class 3 · Proportional group (c): full number resolution
Output amplitude stays proportional to the absorbed energy. The pulse height itself carries the photon number.
•STJ superconducting tunnel junction
•TES transition-edge sensor
•VLPC visible-light photon counter
•QDOGFET quantum-dot FET detector
Where the PMT is used

The PMT is the oldest single-photon detector. It stays the standard where large detector volume, low cost, and room-temperature operation matter. Two examples are particle-physics calorimeters and medical positron-emission-tomography (PET) scanners.

Image sources: sciencetech-inc.com (R4220 tube) · oncologymedicalphysics.com (labelled diagram)

Where the SPAD is used

The SPAD works at room temperature and comes packaged as a small counting module. It is the standard single-photon detector for visible light. Two examples are fluorescence-lifetime microscopy in biology and quantum key distribution over optical fiber.

Image source: Wikimedia Commons, Geek3, CC BY-SA 4.0 · Uses: Hadfield, Nat. Photonics 3, 696 (2009)

Where the SPAD array is used

The silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) is an array of SPADs on one silicon chip. It replaces the photomultiplier tube where compact size, low bias voltage, and insensitivity to magnetic fields matter. Two examples are positron-emission-tomography (PET) scanners in hospitals and light-detection-and-ranging (LIDAR) sensors in cars and smartphones.

Image source: Wikimedia Commons, GLevi, CC BY-SA 3.0 · Uses: Gundacker and Heering, Phys. Med. Biol. 65, 17TR01 (2020)

Where the SNSPD is used

The SNSPD covers the telecom wavelength of 1550 nanometers, where silicon detectors are blind. It is used where photons arrive through long optical fiber or across space. Two examples are quantum key distribution over long fiber links and the Deep Space Optical Communications experiment of NASA, which counts the laser photons from the spacecraft with an SNSPD array.

Image source: NASA/JPL-Caltech, PIA26141, public domain · Uses: Natarajan et al., Supercond. Sci. Technol. 25, 063001 (2012)

Where the STJ is used

The STJ is used where the energy of every single photon must be measured directly. The European Space Agency built a camera around an STJ array and operated it on the William Herschel Telescope: every detected photon received an arrival time and an energy. STJ arrays also work as soft X-ray spectrometers in materials analysis at synchrotron light sources.

Image source: Wikimedia Commons, Tls60, CC BY 3.0 · Uses: Peacock et al., Nature 381, 135 (1996)

Where the VLPC is used

The VLPC counts photons in the visible range and resolves the photon number. Its largest deployment was particle tracking: the D0 experiment at Fermilab read out tens of thousands of scintillating fibers with VLPCs. It also served in quantum optics experiments that need photon-number resolution at high detection efficiency.

Image source: Fermilab / U.S. Department of Energy, public domain · Uses: Abazov et al., Nucl. Instrum. Methods A 565, 463 (2006)
